source_caption:
Homework is one of the most revealing and thought-provoking works by Abbas Kiarostami. On the surface, the film is simple: Kiarostami interviews a group of Iranian schoolchildren about their homework. But as the conversations unfold, it becomes clear that the documentary is about much more than education.

Through a series of direct, often uncomfortable interviews, the children speak about pressure, punishment, fear of failure, and their relationships with parents and teachers. Many struggle to explain why they do homework at all, revealing a system driven more by obedience and anxiety than curiosity or learning.

What makes Homework so powerful is Kiarostami’s approach. He doesn’t lecture or provide easy answers. Instead, he allows the children to speak for themselves, exposing larger questions about authority, childhood, and the way society shapes young minds. The simplicity of the setup only makes the observations more striking.

Like many of Kiarostami’s films, Homework blurs the line between documentary and social reflection. It’s a quiet film, but one that says a great deal about education, family expectations, and the experiences of children whose voices are rarely heard. Decades later, its themes remain just as relevant, making it one of the director’s most insightful and enduring works.

source_details.synopsis: Homework (Persian: مشق شب, romanized: Mašq-e šab) is a 1989 Iranian narrative documentary film written, directed and edited by Abbas Kiarostami. The film was shot on 16mm in late January and/or early February 1988 at Tehran's Shahid Masumi primary school.
